+
+fn reconcile_abandoned_docker_executions(paths: &DeadreckonPaths, job: &Job) -> Result<()> {
+    let directory = paths
+        .job_dir(job.job_id.as_ref())
+        .join("docker-executions");
+    let metadata = match fs::symlink_metadata(&directory) {
+        Ok(metadata) => metadata,
+        Err(source) if source.kind() == std::io::ErrorKind::NotFound => return Ok(()),
+        Err(source) => return Err(source.into()),
+    };
+    if metadata.file_type().is_symlink() || !metadata.file_type().is_dir() {
+        return Err(CliError::Core(DeadreckonError::InvalidInput(format!(
+            "Docker execution records for job {} are not a trusted directory",
+            job.job_id
+        ))));
+    }
+    let mut records = fs::read_dir(&directory)?
+        .collect::<std::result::Result<Vec<_>, _>>()?;
+    records.sort_by_key(fs::DirEntry::file_name);
+    for entry in records {
+        let path = entry.path();
+        if path.extension() != Some(OsStr::new("json")) {
+            continue;
+        }
+        let record = deadreckon_sandbox::read_docker_execution_record(&path)
+            .map_err(|error| CliError::Core(DeadreckonError::InvalidInput(error.to_string())))?;
+        if record.job_id() != job.job_id.as_ref() {
+            return Err(CliError::Core(DeadreckonError::InvalidInput(format!(
+                "Docker execution record {} belongs to a different Job",
+                path.display()
+            ))));
+        }
+        deadreckon_sandbox::reconcile_docker_execution_record(&path)
+            .map_err(|error| CliError::Core(DeadreckonError::InvalidInput(error.to_string())))?;
+        fs::remove_file(&path)?;
+    }
+    Ok(())
+}

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-07-31 07:29:43Z)**_

We have successfully moved DeadReckon from a collection of run/orchestration features toward one coherent durable Job system.

What now works in code:

- `start` creates a durable Job, returns one ID, and detaches supervision.
- Ordinary runs, orchestration, new chains, stored-plan forks, campaigns, and follow-ups enter the same scheduler.
- Jobs have leases, bounded retries, budgets, deadlines, explicit terminal reasons, and recovery logic.
- Graphs and campaigns verify their combined parent result and can repair that parent without rerunning successful child work.
- Completion requires two keys:
  1. deterministic definition-of-done checks;
  2. an independent, read-only semantic judgment.
- A failed check cannot be overruled by the LLM judge. Unavailable or uncertain judging becomes `NEEDS_REVIEW`.
- Successful Jobs produce an HMAC-SHA-256 receipt binding the goal authority, checks, judgment, source, resulting revision, and sandbox evidence.
- Unsafe legacy paths now either enter the Job system or refuse clearly instead of silently using the old conductor.
- The main operator experience has been reduced to `start`, `attach`, `status`, `list`, and `finish`.

We also completed a major hardening pass after discovering that the macOS `dr-gate` binary was being invoked inside Linux Docker. The pending implementation now:

- freezes the exact controller and evaluator binaries into each Job;
- binds their hashes into policy, authority, sandbox observation, and receipt;
- uses static Linux evaluator sidecars inside Docker;
- pins Docker images by immutable image ID and platform;
- records running containers durably so abandoned containers can be recovered or removed;
- packages both Linux architectures’ evaluators with every supported distribution;
- rejects tampered or partially specified evaluator identities.

The committed work has strong automated evidence:

- Three goal commits are already on local `main`.
- The committed workspace suite passed.
- The credential-free adversarial matrix recorded 12 passed, 0 failed, and 9 intentionally unproven live scenarios.
- For the pending Docker/evaluator layer:
  - workspace compilation passed;
  - Docker sandbox tests: 17 passed, 1 live test ignored;
  - packaging/release tests: 40 passed;
  - protocol and receipt tamper tests passed;
  - formatting and the goal-owned diff check are clean.

The honest boundary is that the final product promise is not yet fully proven. The Docker/evaluator hardening remains uncommitted, the full suite must be rerun against it, and the real completion/cancellation/crash/tamper Docker trials are still outstanding. The 20–30 task provider dogfood, active service restart, machine reboot, Linux containment, and signed release rehearsal also remain operator acceptance work.

So the result is: the architecture and most enforcement mechanisms now exist. What remains is integration and real-world proof—not another major redesign. The current truth is documented in [README.md](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/README.md:55), with the remaining acceptance work in [WATCHKEEPER-OPERATOR-ACCEPTANCE.md](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/WATCHKEEPER-OPERATOR-ACCEPTANCE.md:1) and [V1-CANDIDATES.md](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/V1-CANDIDATES.md:3).

+struct PendingJobDirectory {
+    path: PathBuf,
+    armed: bool,
+}
+
+impl PendingJobDirectory {
+    fn create(path: &Path) -> Result<Self> {
+        let parent = path.parent().ok_or_else(|| {
+            CliError::Core(DeadreckonError::InvalidInput(format!(
+                "Job directory has no parent: {}",
+                path.display()
+            )))
+        })?;
+        fs::create_dir_all(parent)?;
+        fs::create_dir(path)?;
+        #[cfg(unix)]
+        fs::File::open(parent)?.sync_all()?;
+        Ok(Self {
+            path: path.to_path_buf(),
+            armed: true,
+        })
+    }
+
+    fn commit(mut self) {
+        self.armed = false;
+    }
+}
+
+impl Drop for PendingJobDirectory {
+    fn drop(&mut self) {
+        if !self.armed {
+            return;
+        }
+        let _ = fs::remove_dir_all(&self.path);
+        #[cfg(unix)]
+        if let Some(parent) = self.path.parent() {
+            let _ = fs::File::open(parent).and_then(|directory| directory.sync_all());
+        }
+    }
+}

+#[cfg(unix)]
+#[test]
+#[ignore = "requires DEADRECKON_LIVE_DOCKER_TEST=1, a running daemon, cached rust:1, and the static Linux evaluator sidecar"]
+fn live_docker_public_cancel_removes_container_record_and_prevents_retry() {
+    require_live_docker_test();
+    let fixture = launch_live_docker_job(
+        "Enter the approved cancellable Docker gate.",
+        r#"name: cancellable Docker gate
+checks:
+  - kind: shell
+    command: |
+      set -eu
+      : > "$PWD/gate-ready"
+      while :; do sleep 1; done
+    cwd: "{working_dir}"
+"#,
+    );
+    wait_for_job_path(
+        &fixture.paths,
+        &fixture.job_id,
+        &fixture.state.working_dir.join("gate-ready"),
+        Duration::from_secs(60),
+    );
+    let container = wait_for_docker_container(&fixture.job_id, Duration::from_secs(20));
+    let record_path = wait_for_gate_record(&fixture.state.run_root, Duration::from_secs(10));
+
+    let cancelled = public_deadreckon()
+        .current_dir(&fixture.workspace)
+        .env("DEADRECKON_HOME", fixture.paths.home())
+        .args(["kill", &fixture.job_id, "--escalate", "--plain"])
+        .output()
+        .expect("public cancel");
+    assert!(
+        cancelled.status.success(),
+        "stdout:\n{}\nstderr:\n{}",
+        String::from_utf8_lossy(&cancelled.stdout),
+        String::from_utf8_lossy(&cancelled.stderr)
+    );
+
+    let view = wait_for_terminal_job(&fixture.paths, &fixture.job_id, Duration::from_secs(60));
+    assert_eq!(view.projection.outcome, Some(JobOutcome::Cancelled));
+    wait_for_docker_container_exit(&container, Duration::from_secs(20));
+    assert!(
+        !record_path.exists(),
+        "guarded evaluator record survived cancellation"
+    );
+    assert!(
+        !deadreckon_core::marker_path_for_run_root(&fixture.state.run_root).exists(),
+        "cancelled Docker gate wrote a deterministic marker"
+    );
+    assert!(
+        !fixture.paths.job_receipt(&fixture.job_id).exists(),
+        "cancelled Docker gate wrote a completion receipt"
+    );
+    let history = deadreckon_core::read_job_history(
+        &fixture.paths.job_events(&fixture.job_id),
+    )
+    .expect("job history");
+    let cancel_index = history
+        .events()
+        .iter()
+        .position(|event| event.kind == JobEventKind::CancelRequested)
+        .expect("CancelRequested");
+    assert!(
+        history.events()[cancel_index + 1..]
+            .iter()
+            .all(|event| event.kind != JobEventKind::RetryScheduled),
+        "a retry was scheduled after operator cancellation"
+    );
+    assert_docker_job_clean(&fixture);
+}

+#[test]
+#[ignore = "requires DEADRECKON_LIVE_DOCKER_TEST=1, a running daemon, cached rust:1, and the static Linux evaluator sidecar"]
+fn live_docker_worker_sigkill_reconciles_stale_container_before_one_retry() {
+    require_live_docker_test();
+    let fixture = launch_live_docker_job(
+        "Recover the approved Docker gate after one worker crash.",
+        r#"name: recoverable Docker gate
+checks:
+  - kind: shell
+    command: |
+      set -eu
+      if test ! -f "$PWD/first-gate-attempt"; then
+        : > "$PWD/first-gate-attempt"
+        : > "$PWD/gate-ready"
+        while :; do sleep 1; done
+      fi
+    cwd: "{working_dir}"
+"#,
+    );
+    wait_for_job_path(
+        &fixture.paths,
+        &fixture.job_id,
+        &fixture.state.working_dir.join("gate-ready"),
+        Duration::from_secs(60),
+    );
+    let first_container = wait_for_docker_container(&fixture.job_id, Duration::from_secs(20));
+    let outer =
+        read_supervised_process(&fixture.paths.job_dir(&fixture.job_id).join("supervised-child.json"))
+            .expect("outer supervised worker");
+    signal_pid(outer.pid, nix::sys::signal::Signal::SIGKILL);
+
+    let deadline = Instant::now() + Duration::from_secs(90);
+    let view = loop {
+        let containers = docker_job_containers(&fixture.job_id);
+        assert!(
+            containers.len() <= 1,
+            "retry launched before the stale Docker container was reconciled: {containers:?}"
+        );
+        if let Ok(view) = JobView::load(&fixture.paths, &fixture.job_id)
+            && view.projection.is_terminal()
+        {
+            break view;
+        }
+        assert!(
+            Instant::now() < deadline,
+            "Job {} did not recover after worker SIGKILL\nsupervisor stderr:\n{}",
+            fixture.job_id,
+            fixture.supervisor_stderr()
+        );
+        thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(50));
+    };
+
+    assert_eq!(view.projection.outcome, Some(JobOutcome::NeedsReview));
+    wait_for_docker_container_exit(&first_container, Duration::from_secs(20));
+    let history = deadreckon_core::read_job_history(
+        &fixture.paths.job_events(&fixture.job_id),
+    )
+    .expect("job history");
+    assert_eq!(
+        history
+            .events()
+            .iter()
+            .filter(|event| event.kind == JobEventKind::RetryScheduled)
+            .count(),
+        1,
+        "the interrupted attempt should schedule exactly one bounded retry"
+    );
+    assert!(
+        deadreckon_core::marker_path_for_run_root(&fixture.state.run_root).exists(),
+        "the retry did not complete deterministic Docker verification"
+    );
+    assert!(
+        !fixture.paths.job_receipt(&fixture.job_id).exists(),
+        "the smoke semantic transport must not issue a completion receipt"
+    );
+    assert_docker_job_clean(&fixture);
+}

+#[cfg(unix)]
+fn docker_job_containers(job_id: &str) -> Vec<String> {
+    let filter = format!("label=io.deadreckon.job-id={job_id}");
+    let output = Command::new("docker")
+        .args(["ps", "-aq", "--filter", &filter])
+        .output()
+        .expect("docker ps");
+    assert!(
+        output.status.success(),
+        "docker ps failed: {}",
+        String::from_utf8_lossy(&output.stderr)
+    );
+    String::from_utf8_lossy(&output.stdout)
+        .lines()
+        .map(str::trim)
+        .filter(|line| !line.is_empty())
+        .map(str::to_string)
+        .collect()
+}
+
+#[cfg(unix)]
+fn wait_for_docker_container(job_id: &str, timeout: Duration) -> String {
+    let deadline = Instant::now() + timeout;
+    loop {
+        let containers = docker_job_containers(job_id);
+        if let [container] = containers.as_slice() {
+            return container.clone();
+        }
+        assert!(
+            Instant::now() < deadline,
+            "Docker container for Job {job_id} was not observed: {containers:?}"
+        );
+        thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(25));
+    }
+}
+
+#[cfg(unix)]
+fn wait_for_docker_container_exit(container: &str, timeout: Duration) {
+    let deadline = Instant::now() + timeout;
+    loop {
+        let output = Command::new("docker")
+            .args(["container", "inspect", container])
+            .output()
+            .expect("docker inspect");
+        if !output.status.success() {
+            return;
+        }
+        assert!(
+            Instant::now() < deadline,
+            "Docker container {container} remained after cleanup"
+        );
+        thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(25));
+    }
+}
+
+#[cfg(unix)]
+fn assert_docker_job_clean(fixture: &LiveDockerFixture) {
+    assert!(

+        "managed Docker container survived terminal Job state"
+    );
+    assert!(

+                .paths
+                .job_dir(&fixture.job_id)
+                .join("docker-executions")
+        ),
+        "durable Docker recovery records survived terminal Job state"
+    );

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-07-31 07:53:39Z)**_

The daemon run exposed a real integration bug, not a test issue: the durable container record lived under the Job, but its Docker CID file was created there while the guarded process record lived under the Run. The sandbox correctly rejected that split identity. I’m keeping the durable recovery record under the Job while placing the CID beside its guarded process record, so both identities remain linked and crash recovery still finds them through the Job record.

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-07-31 08:05:47Z)**_

The honest summary: we have successfully built most of DeadReckon’s core execution and verification model. We have not yet proven the complete “survives every interruption unattended” promise.

Successfully implemented and verified:

- A durable job model with persistent state, leasing, retries, recovery information and explicit terminal outcomes.
- A mostly unified lifecycle for runs, chains and plans, exposed through the simpler job-oriented CLI.
- Append-only lifecycle events from which current job state can be reconstructed.
- Deterministic definition-of-done checks plus an independent semantic judge.
- Fail-closed verification: failed checks cannot be overruled, and unavailable or uncertain semantic judgment produces `NEEDS_REVIEW`.
- HMAC-protected gate observations and receipts bound to the contract, policy, source revision, result revision and evaluator identity.
- Signing keys and protected proof paths kept outside the agent-visible workspace.
- Frozen controller and evaluator binaries, with detection of replacement, symlink and identity tampering.
- Isolated worktrees and Docker evaluator execution using immutable image identities.
- Durable Docker execution records and supervisor reconciliation logic.
- Release packaging that includes the required native helpers and Linux evaluator sidecars.
- Extensive focused testing of partial identity data, receipt tampering, frozen-binary tampering, job creation rollback, evaluator identity echoing and release contents.
- A real Docker end-to-end completion run passed: checks executed inside the isolated boundary, the signed observation was accepted, and an uncertain semantic result correctly stopped at `NEEDS_REVIEW`.

Integration status:

- Three substantial commits are already on local `main`:
  - `9b786d8` — durable verification boundaries
  - `39faddd` — remaining product boundaries
  - `9423648` — adversarial evidence bound to clean source
- Local `main` is three commits ahead of `origin/main`.
- A further Docker, evaluator-freezing and release-packaging layer is implemented but remains uncommitted while verification continues.

What is not yet successfully finished:

- The live Docker cancellation test currently fails because the evaluator container survives cancellation. I verified and removed only that test-created container.
- The worker-`SIGKILL` recovery test has not yet been proven green.
- The complete workspace test suite and final schema/release verification still need to run.
- Documentation and operator acceptance instructions need reconciliation.
- The promised 20–30 real-task dogfood campaign has not happened.
- Reboot/service recovery, Linux sandbox testing, real-provider semantic judging and signed release CI remain unproven.
- The pending changes still need a clean scope audit, commit and eventual push.

So the achievement is substantial: DeadReckon now has a coherent durable executor, independent verification system and hardened trust boundary. The remaining work is less about inventing the architecture and more about proving that interruption cleanup, recovery, packaging and real-world operation hold together reliably. The goal should remain active until those proofs are complete.

name: diagnose-before-edit
description: Use when behavior is surprising, a fix failed, or the territory is unfamiliar — suspend edits, trace the end-to-end mechanism, and prove WHERE and WHY before changing any code.
---

# Diagnose Before Edit

When something is misbehaving or you are in unfamiliar code, do not patch the symptom. Impose a read-only gate: name and trace the mechanism first, locate the fault, and only edit once the cause is pinned to specific files. This mirrors the user's standing practice of fusing an explicit "don't write any code yet" constraint to a "help me understand how X works" demand.

## Steps

1. Treat a "step back", "don't change anything yet", "where does X happen", or "how does this work" cue (explicit or implied by a surprising bug) as a switch into read-only diagnosis. Do not edit code in this phase.
2. Trace the end-to-end mechanism and narrate it: where the value/behavior originates, every hop it takes, and where it finally renders or takes effect. Name the specific files and lines.
3. Localize the fault before proposing any fix. State which location(s) you suspect and the evidence for that localization — and check whether it could live in more than one place rather than assuming a single site.
4. State the causal chain explicitly and, when rejecting a candidate fix, supply a competing root-cause hypothesis rather than just trying again.
5. Propose how the fix will be verified, then wait for authorization before editing.
6. Only after the mechanism's home is pinned to concrete files, make the minimal change at that layer — never patch the layer where the symptom merely surfaced.

## Verification

Before editing, you should be able to answer, in writing: "The behavior is produced by `<file>:<lines>` because `<causal chain>`, and I will confirm the fix by `<observation/command>`." If you cannot, you have not finished diagnosing.

## Failure modes

- Patching the layer where the symptom appears (e.g. button-state code) when the real cause is elsewhere (a default selection upstream). The user rejects this with: "You got it wrong… the issue was not with the button states." Localize first.
- Jumping to a fix on the first plausible theory. Demand or construct the observation that would discriminate between candidate causes before committing to one.
- Editing during a "don't write any code yet" instruction. That instruction is a gate, not a delay — produce the mechanism trace and stop.

## Notes

Forged by Lore from latent practice across specstory-monorepo and stoa (2024-12 → 2026-04), consistently followed by the user, high adjacent-approval rate. Consolidates the read-before-write gate, fault-localization-before-fix, and mechanism-trace-before-trust patterns.

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-07-31 08:07:46Z)**_

The cause is now pinned down. Docker records are written under the Job before launch, but cancellation only reconciles host process records before declaring `Cancelled`. Cooperative runtime cleanup never runs when the outer worker is force-killed, and the only durable Docker recovery hook currently runs before a future attempt—which a terminal cancelled job will never have. The fix belongs in Job cancellation finalization, before the terminal event; I’ll verify it with the same public live-Docker test and then the worker-`SIGKILL` recovery test. The active goal already authorizes that implementation.

+pub(crate) fn reconcile_job_docker_executions(
+    paths: &DeadreckonPaths,
+    job: &Job,
+) -> Result<()> {
+    let directory = paths.job_dir(job.job_id.as_ref()).join("docker-executions");
+    let metadata = match fs::symlink_metadata(&directory) {
+        Ok(metadata) => metadata,
+        Err(source) if source.kind() == std::io::ErrorKind::NotFound => return Ok(()),
+        Err(source) => return Err(source.into()),
+    };
+    if metadata.file_type().is_symlink() || !metadata.file_type().is_dir() {
+        return Err(CliError::Core(DeadreckonError::InvalidInput(format!(
+            "Docker execution records for job {} are not a trusted directory",
+            job.job_id
+        ))));
+    }
+    let mut records = fs::read_dir(&directory)?.collect::<std::result::Result<Vec<_>, _>>()?;
+    records.sort_by_key(fs::DirEntry::file_name);
+    for entry in records {
+        let path = entry.path();
+        if path.extension() != Some(OsStr::new("json")) {
+            continue;
+        }
+        let record = deadreckon_sandbox::read_docker_execution_record(&path)
+            .map_err(|error| CliError::Core(DeadreckonError::InvalidInput(error.to_string())))?;
+        if record.job_id() != job.job_id.as_ref() {
+            return Err(CliError::Core(DeadreckonError::InvalidInput(format!(
+                "Docker execution record {} belongs to a different Job",
+                path.display()
+            ))));
+        }
+        deadreckon_sandbox::reconcile_docker_execution_record(&path)
+            .map_err(|error| CliError::Core(DeadreckonError::InvalidInput(error.to_string())))?;
+    }
+    Ok(())
+}

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-07-31 08:51:20Z)**_

We have successfully built most of the core DeadReckon execution promise. This is no longer only a design.

What now works:

- A durable job lifecycle backed by append-only events, leases and explicit terminal reasons such as completed, blocked, cancelled, failed and budget exhausted.
- Detached supervision with abandoned-lease recovery, crash-atomic child launches and bounded retries.
- Runs, plans, chains and campaigns increasingly converge on the same durable Job machinery. Legacy chain mutation paths have been closed or moved behind compatibility boundaries.
- Deterministic completion checks are followed by an independent, read-only semantic judge. The judge returns achieved, revise or uncertain; it cannot override failed checks.
- Completed child work can be retained while only failed semantic-parent work is repaired.
- Gate signing material is kept outside the agent workspace. Receipts are bound to the contract, policy, source/result revisions, evaluator identity and observed sandbox boundary.
- Synthetic evidence, altered frozen binaries, forged markers, policy drift, stale judgments and protected-path tampering are rejected.
- Docker executions now have durable ownership records. Cancellation and worker death clean up containers before recording a truthful terminal state or retrying.
- Operator capture and evidence records were added so trials can be authenticated and reproduced.
- The release pipeline is being extended to package the trusted helper binaries and Linux evaluator sidecars.

The strongest successful proofs are:

- The complete `cargo test --workspace --all-targets` run has just finished with exit code 0. Every non-live test passed.
- The checked-in schema drift test passed.
- Three separate live Docker trials passed:
  - normal verified execution;
  - operator cancellation with no receipt or retry;
  - worker `SIGKILL`, stale-container recovery and exactly one bounded retry.
- No DeadReckon-managed containers were left behind.
- The committed credential-free adversarial matrix records 12 passed scenarios tied to a clean source revision.

The honest boundary is that the goal is not completely closed:

- The latest Docker, evaluator-identity and release-packaging hardening remains uncommitted.
- Local `main` is three commits ahead of `origin/main`; nothing from those commits has been pushed.
- We still need final formatting/check/release-script validation, documentation reconciliation and a clean scoped commit.
- We have not yet completed the promised 20–30 real tasks across repositories and providers.
- A real-provider semantic `Achieved` receipt, service/reboot survival, Linux sandbox trials and cross-platform signed release verification remain outstanding.

So the present assessment is: **the durable, isolated, independently verified execution architecture is substantially implemented and passing its automated and Docker failure tests. The remaining work is mainly integration, release hardening, and broader real-world proof—not invention of the core system.**

#[test]
#[ignore = "requires DEADRECKON_LIVE_DOCKER_TEST=1, a running daemon, cached rust:1, and the static Linux evaluator sidecar"]
fn live_docker_public_job_completes_deterministic_gate_and_cleans_daemon_state() {
    require_live_docker_test();
    let fixture = launch_live_docker_job(
        "Complete the approved deterministic Docker gate.",
        r#"name: Docker completion
checks:
  - kind: file_exists
    path: "{working_dir}/README.md"
"#,
    );

    let view = wait_for_terminal_job(&fixture.paths, &fixture.job_id, Duration::from_secs(90));
    assert_eq!(
        view.projection.outcome,
        Some(JobOutcome::NeedsReview),
        "the smoke semantic transport must fail closed after the real Docker gate\n\
         diagnostics:\n{}",
        fixture.diagnostics()
    );
    let state = load_run(&fixture.paths, &fixture.job_id).expect("Job result run");
    let marker = validate_acceptance_marker(&state).expect("trusted Docker gate marker");
    assert!(marker.is_native_gate_proof(), "{marker:#?}");
    assert!(marker.contained, "{marker:#?}");
    assert_eq!(marker.sandbox_backend, "docker");
    assert_eq!(marker.check_count, 1);
    assert!(marker.checks.iter().all(|check| check.passed));

    let authority: JobAuthority = serde_json::from_slice(
        &fs::read(fixture.paths.job_authority(&fixture.job_id)).expect("Job authority"),
    )
    .expect("Job authority JSON");
    let observation =
        validate_sandbox_boundary_observation(&fixture.paths, &state, &authority, "docker")
            .expect("controller-signed Docker boundary observation");
    assert!(observation.contained);
    assert!(observation.gate_key_read_denied);
    assert!(observation.proof_write_denied);
    assert!(observation.control_write_denied);
    assert!(observation.operator_capture_read_denied);
    assert!(observation.operator_capture_write_denied);
    assert!(observation.signing_env_scrubbed);
    assert_eq!(
        observation.gate_evaluator_sha256,
        authority.gate_evaluator_sha256
    );

    let job = deadreckon_core::load_job(&fixture.paths, &fixture.job_id).expect("Job");
    let docker = job
        .policy
        .execution
        .as_ref()
        .and_then(|execution| execution.gate_evaluator.as_ref())
        .and_then(|identity| identity.docker.as_ref())
        .expect("immutable Docker evaluator identity");
    assert!(docker.image_id.starts_with("sha256:"));
    assert_eq!(docker.platform, "linux/arm64");
    assert_eq!(
        docker.guest_path,
        Path::new(deadreckon_protocol::DOCKER_GATE_GUEST_PATH)
    );
    assert!(
        gate_key_path(&fixture.paths, &fixture.job_id).is_file(),
        "signing material must remain outside the evaluator-visible workspace"
    );
    assert!(
        !fixture.paths.job_receipt(&fixture.job_id).exists(),
        "the smoke semantic transport must not issue a trusted receipt"
    );
    assert_docker_job_clean(&fixture);
}

---
name: operator-acceptance-checklist
description: Use when an implementation phase lands (or before declaring work done) — convert what was built into a concrete, plain-language manual test script the human runs from the operator's seat, instead of claiming completion yourself.
---

# Operator Acceptance Checklist

Completion is never the agent's to declare. At every phase boundary, translate the work into observable, operator-POV confirmation steps the human can execute by hand — which commands they can now run, what should look different, what to check. The human running those steps is the acceptance gate; the agent's report is not.

## Steps

1. At kickoff of any multi-phase build, establish the contract: "When there is something to build and test, stop and describe in plain language the functionality implemented, open questions, and exactly what to test."
2. When a phase is done, do NOT say "done" or just summarize the diff. Produce a manual test script.
3. The script must be operator-POV and concrete:
   - The exact commands to run (with working directory).
   - The new capability the user can now exercise end-to-end.
   - The specific, observable signal that confirms success (a journal/db entry, a UI change, a log line, a returned value).
   - What is explicitly NOT yet covered, so scope is honest.
4. Prefer real, runnable verification (a CLI invocation, a SQL/inspection command, a screen to open) over abstract description.
5. Hand the script to the user and wait — they verify by hand before the work is accepted.

## Verification

The deliverable of a phase is the test script itself. It passes the bar when a person who did not write the code could follow it start-to-finish and observe each success signal without asking a follow-up question.

## Failure modes

- Reporting "this should work" or pasting a diff as if it were acceptance. The user's response is "so what should i be able to test right now" / "explain clearly what I should be able to functionally test" — pre-empt it.
- Listing what changed in code terms instead of what the operator can now do and see.
- Omitting the not-yet-covered list, which hides scope and erodes trust in the checklist.

## Notes

Forged by Lore from latent practice in stoa (2025-10 → 2026-03), a recurrent and verified acceptance discipline. Consolidates the manual-test-script demand, operator-seat acceptance, and user-POV verification contract.
```

# Watchkeeper operator acceptance

Status: ready to run; no live trial is claimed by this document.

This is the human acceptance script for Watchkeeper. Run it from disposable
repository clones with providers whose spend you have approved. A checked box
means an operator observed the stated signal; passing repository tests does not
check these boxes automatically.

## What this accepts

The current acceptance boundary is:

- guided `start` and ordinary direct execution create a durable Job before work
  and return one parent ID;
- durable Single, Graph and Campaign Jobs require a contained deterministic
  pass, semantic `achieved` and a valid parent receipt before promotion;
- durable Graph work always delivers at the end and verifies the same-ID merged
  parent;
- durable Campaign work can recover an exactly linked persisted sub-plan and
  revalidates its worst-of roll-up before parent verification;
- ordinary direct `run` and `orchestrate`, new supported chains, stored-plan
  `fork`, and direct campaigns share the durable Job scheduler;
- public `extend` and a follow-up selected by guided `start` create a durable
  parent-bound Single Job;
- previews, explicit in-place/uncontained execution, historical `chain
  run|resume`, unsupported conductor policies, and chain extension remain
  process-owned compatibility paths;
- launchd/systemd definitions and commands exist, but machine recovery becomes
  an accepted claim only after the live drill below.

## Safety and prerequisites

Use two disposable clones. `finish` changes the selected checkout. Do not use a
valued working tree or the normal production state directory.

```bash
cd /path/to/deadreckon
cargo build --release

export WK_BIN="$PWD/target/release/deadreckon"
export WK_STATE="/path/to/disposable/watchkeeper-state"
export WK_REPO_A="/path/to/disposable/deadreckon-clone"
export WK_REPO_B="/path/to/disposable/fixture-app"
export WK_PROVIDER_A="cli:codex"
export WK_PROVIDER_B="cli:claude-code"
export WK_ARTIFACTS="$WK_STATE/operator-captures/dogfood"
export DR_CAPTURE_BIN="$PWD/target/release/dr-capture"
export DEADRECKON_BIN="$WK_BIN"

test -x "$WK_BIN"
test -x "$DR_CAPTURE_BIN"
test -d "$WK_REPO_A/.git"
test -d "$WK_REPO_B/.git"
mkdir -p "$WK_STATE"
mkdir -p "$WK_ARTIFACTS"
export DEADRECKON_HOME="$WK_STATE"
"$WK_BIN" doctor
```

Before spending money, confirm both repositories have an approved definition
of done and the host reports at least one real sandbox backend:

```bash
cd "$WK_REPO_A"
"$WK_BIN" def-done show
"$WK_BIN" def-done check
cd "$WK_REPO_B"
"$WK_BIN" def-done show
"$WK_BIN" def-done check
"$WK_BIN" doctor --json
"$WK_BIN" run --preview "operator acceptance preflight"
```

Expected signal: `doctor --json` reports `sandbox-exec`, `bwrap`, or `docker`
with `available: true`, and the preview's requested sandbox is `auto` or that
explicit backend, not `none`. Preview records the request; the supervisor
records the resolved backend when it runs. A strict Job that resolves to
`none` is expected to stop for review, not verify.

## Record every live fault claim

Prepare the passive recorder after creating the disposable Job for each fault
drill and before the intervention. It records evidence but never starts a
provider, signals a process, changes networking, controls the service, reboots,
or calls `finish`. The operator remains responsible for the reviewed fault and
cleanup.

Pass-capable recording requires the protected `dr-capture` and sibling
`deadreckon` binaries to remain outside every Job source, working, run, merge
and repair root. For example, before section 3:

```bash
export WK_TRIAL_ID=live_provider_supervisor_restart
export WK_LIVE_TRIAL="$WK_ARTIFACTS/live/$WK_TRIAL_ID-01"
export WK_JOB_ID=the-full-approved-job-id

python3 examples/watchkeeper-dogfood/live-trial.py prepare \
  "$WK_TRIAL_ID" \
  --trial-dir "$WK_LIVE_TRIAL" \
  --revision "$(git rev-parse HEAD)" \
  --capture-helper "$DR_CAPTURE_BIN" \
  --deadreckon-binary "$DEADRECKON_BIN" \
  --job-id "$WK_JOB_ID" \
  --backend sandbox-exec \
  --provider-route worker="$WK_PROVIDER_A" \
  --provider-route independent_judge="$WK_PROVIDER_B"
python3 -m json.tool "$WK_LIVE_TRIAL/replay.json"
```

Use the backend that the strict Job actually resolved. The provider roles must
match the manifest and the worker and independent judge must be different.
Preparation is retry-safe for identical inputs and refuses a conflicting
binding.
```

---
name: diagnose-before-edit
description: Use when behavior is surprising, a fix failed, or the territory is unfamiliar — suspend edits, trace the end-to-end mechanism, and prove WHERE and WHY before changing any code.
---

# Diagnose Before Edit

When something is misbehaving or you are in unfamiliar code, do not patch the symptom. Impose a read-only gate: name and trace the mechanism first, locate the fault, and only edit once the cause is pinned to specific files. This mirrors the user's standing practice of fusing an explicit "don't write any code yet" constraint to a "help me understand how X works" demand.

## Steps

1. Treat a "step back", "don't change anything yet", "where does X happen", or "how does this work" cue (explicit or implied by a surprising bug) as a switch into read-only diagnosis. Do not edit code in this phase.
2. Trace the end-to-end mechanism and narrate it: where the value/behavior originates, every hop it takes, and where it finally renders or takes effect. Name the specific files and lines.
3. Localize the fault before proposing any fix. State which location(s) you suspect and the evidence for that localization — and check whether it could live in more than one place rather than assuming a single site.
4. State the causal chain explicitly and, when rejecting a candidate fix, supply a competing root-cause hypothesis rather than just trying again.
5. Propose how the fix will be verified, then wait for authorization before editing.
6. Only after the mechanism's home is pinned to concrete files, make the minimal change at that layer — never patch the layer where the symptom merely surfaced.

## Verification

Before editing, you should be able to answer, in writing: "The behavior is produced by `<file>:<lines>` because `<causal chain>`, and I will confirm the fix by `<observation/command>`." If you cannot, you have not finished diagnosing.

## Failure modes

- Patching the layer where the symptom appears (e.g. button-state code) when the real cause is elsewhere (a default selection upstream). The user rejects this with: "You got it wrong… the issue was not with the button states." Localize first.
- Jumping to a fix on the first plausible theory. Demand or construct the observation that would discriminate between candidate causes before committing to one.
- Editing during a "don't write any code yet" instruction. That instruction is a gate, not a delay — produce the mechanism trace and stop.

## Notes

Forged by Lore from latent practice across specstory-monorepo and stoa (2024-12 → 2026-04), consistently followed by the user, high adjacent-approval rate. Consolidates the read-before-write gate, fault-localization-before-fix, and mechanism-trace-before-trust patterns.

struct MergeRepairRunRecordUpdate<'a> {
    run_id: &'a str,
    status: &'a str,
    repair_id: &'a str,
    repair_round: u32,
    repair_request_sha256: &'a str,
    repair_plan_sha256: &'a str,
    sandbox_requested: deadreckon_sandbox::SandboxBackend,
    planner_spend_usd: f64,
    planner_wall_seconds: f64,
}

fn write_merge_repair_run_record(
    paths: &DeadreckonPaths,
    plan: &Plan,
    context: &MergeRepairContext,
    update: MergeRepairRunRecordUpdate<'_>,
) -> Result<()> {
    let path = context.proof_dir.join("repair-run.json");
    let state = load_run(paths, update.run_id).ok();
    let mut value: Value = serde_json::from_slice(&fs::read(&path)?)?;
    let object = value.as_object_mut().ok_or_else(|| {
        CliError::Core(DeadreckonError::InvalidInput(
            "merge repair launch authority is not an object".to_string(),
        ))
    })?;
    if object.get("plan_id").and_then(Value::as_str) != Some(plan.plan_id.as_str())
        || object.get("repair_id").and_then(Value::as_str) != Some(update.repair_id)
        || object.get("repair_round").and_then(Value::as_u64)
            != Some(u64::from(update.repair_round))
        || object.get("repair_request_sha256").and_then(Value::as_str)
            != Some(update.repair_request_sha256)
        || object.get("repair_plan_sha256").and_then(Value::as_str)
            != Some(update.repair_plan_sha256)
        || object.get("sandbox_requested").and_then(Value::as_str)
            != Some(update.sandbox_requested.to_string().as_str())
        || object
            .get("run_id")
            .and_then(Value::as_str)
            .is_some_and(|existing| existing != update.run_id)
    {
        return Err(CliError::Core(DeadreckonError::InvalidInput(
            "merge repair completion crossed its durable launch authority".to_string(),
        )));
    }
    object.insert(
        "run_id".to_string(),
        Value::String(update.run_id.to_string()),
    );
    object.insert(
        "scope".to_string(),
        serde_json::to_value(state.as_ref().map(|state| state.scope.clone()))?,
    );
    object.insert(
        "status".to_string(),
        Value::String(update.status.to_string()),
    );
    object.insert(
        "planner_spend_usd".to_string(),
        serde_json::to_value(update.planner_spend_usd)?,
    );
    object.insert(
        "planner_wall_seconds".to_string(),
        serde_json::to_value(update.planner_wall_seconds)?,
    );
    object.insert("updated_at".to_string(), serde_json::to_value(Utc::now())?);
    commands::job::replace_json_synced(&path, &value)
}

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-07-31 09:49:05Z)**_

The core promise is now substantially implemented and working locally—not merely designed.

Successfully completed:

- Durable jobs with leases, heartbeats, fencing and append-only lifecycle events.
- Recovery after worker death without duplicating attempts or accepting stale writes.
- Explicit outcomes for cancelled, blocked, failed, budget/time exhausted, retry exhausted and needs review.
- Plans and campaigns operate beneath one durable job identity with ownership checks and crash repair.
- Two-key completion:
  1. deterministic acceptance checks must pass;
  2. an independent, read-only semantic judge must return evidence-backed `achieved`.
- Strict mode fails to `NEEDS REVIEW` when semantic verification or receipt sealing is unavailable.
- HMAC-SHA-256 receipts with signing keys outside agent-visible workspaces.
- Receipts bind the contract, policy, source/result revisions, evidence, evaluator identity and resulting deliverable tree.
- Gate, proof and repository-control paths are protected against hostile workers.
- Strict Docker execution uses immutable image identity, static evaluator sidecars and durable container records.
- Release packaging now includes the native helpers and Linux evaluator sidecars, with installer/signing verification support.
- Operator and architecture documentation has been updated, including the [acceptance checklist](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/WATCHKEEPER-OPERATOR-ACCEPTANCE.md).

Most importantly, we have real interruption evidence:

- Normal Docker completion: passed.
- Operator cancellation: passed and prevented retry.
- Worker `SIGKILL`: passed, reconciled the abandoned container and performed exactly one retry.
- No DeadReckon-managed containers remained afterward.

The complete `cargo test --workspace --all-targets` run passed, including the large durability, recovery, tampering, semantic-judge and ownership suites. Formatting and canonical Clippy also pass.

What remains:

- Commit the final verified working-tree changes.
- Generate new clean-source adversarial evidence tied to that commit.
- Push/integrate the work upstream. Three goal commits are already on local `main`, but nothing from this latest layer has been pushed.
- Run the promised 20–30 real tasks across repositories and providers.
- Prove restart after a machine reboot or installed supervisor-service restart.
- Complete Linux/bubblewrap and real network-loss trials.
- Exercise actual macOS/Windows signing, notarization and release publication.
- Measure false acceptance, false rejection, intervention rate and judging cost.

So the honest assessment is: **the core mechanism now works and survives deliberate process/container interruption, but the wider operational proof and release integration are not finished.**

Diagnosis is pinned: `dist-workspace.toml` enables GitHub hosting metadata, while the read-only `dist-plan` job calls `dist host --steps=create`, which attempts a release mutation before trust artifacts exist. A later write-scoped job already owns release creation with `gh`. The correct boundary is therefore: `dist plan` remains read-only on every ref; only the final publish job creates or updates GitHub releases. I’ll verify that with a regression assertion plus workflow/YAML and release tests.

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-07-31 10:43:30Z)**_

We have successfully built the core of the promised DeadReckon model.

What now works:

- Goals start as durable local jobs with stable IDs and isolated workspaces.
- Jobs detach, hold leases, recover abandoned work, and retry within explicit bounds.
- Worker and supervisor crashes are handled without duplicating the logical attempt.
- Cancellation stops the contained process and cannot accidentally produce a completion receipt.
- Runs, graphs/chains, plans and campaigns now pass through the same durable job ownership boundary.
- Completion requires both deterministic checks and an independent semantic judgment.
- A missing or invalid semantic judgment fails closed as `needs review`; deterministic success alone cannot claim completion.
- Semantic `revise` decisions and bounded parent repair are implemented and tested.
- Gate evaluation is isolated from receipt signing. Agent-visible code cannot access the signing key or forge trusted completion.
- Receipts bind the goal contract, source revision, resulting revision, evaluator identity and evidence.
- Mutation, symlink substitution, stale evidence, result-tree changes and attempted receipt forgery are rejected.
- Docker-backed execution now records durable container identity, cleans up after cancellation and recovers correctly after a worker is killed.
- Release ownership was tightened so planning remains read-only and GitHub release mutation happens only after trust and attestation checks.
- The operator-facing `start`, `status`, `attach`, `finish` and receipt journey is covered by the dogfood harness.

The strongest clean-source evidence currently reports:

- 13 trials passed
- 0 failed
- 8 explicitly unproven
- All three public Docker trials passed: normal completion, cancellation and crash recovery
- The evidence was generated from an exact clean commit rather than the working directory

The implementation is integrated into six commits on the local `main` branch, currently ending at `761b001`. It has not been pushed to `origin/main`.

Verification completed includes formatting, strict Clippy, release builds, binary-size checks, 133 release-mode chain tests, 180 release-mode orchestration tests, the Docker trials and the dogfood validation suite. A final repeat of the entire workspace suite is still running and everything completed so far is green.

What we have not yet proved is the full real-world promise:

- 20–30 genuine tasks across providers and repositories
- Paid-provider interruption and network-loss recovery
- Recovery through a real machine reboot and installed user service
- A hostile cross-provider gate attack
- A naturally occurring semantic `revise` and repair
- A live Campaign interrupted and recovered
- Linux/bubblewrap execution
- Actual Apple/Windows signing, notarization and release publication

So the honest verdict is: **the architecture and its local adversarial proof are substantially implemented; the remaining work is mostly operational validation across real providers, machines and release platforms.**

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-07-31 11:29:18Z)**_

We have successfully built the core of the promised DeadReckon model. The remaining work is mostly real-world acceptance and integration—not another architectural rewrite.

What now works:

- `start` creates a detached, durable Job with an ID.
- Jobs have append-only event history, fenced leases and restart recovery.
- Worker and supervisor interruption recovery is implemented.
- Attempts, time and spend are bounded.
- Terminal states distinguish failure, cancellation, blocking and budget exhaustion.
- Runs, plans, chains and campaigns now converge on the same durable Job scheduler.
- Completion requires deterministic checks plus an independent semantic judgment.
- Semantic repair for parent Graph/Campaign Jobs is durable and does not rerun successful children.
- The gate is isolated from the worker, uses protected HMAC signing and fails closed.
- Receipts bind the contract, policy, source revision, result revision, evidence and sandbox observations.
- Promotion and result delivery require a valid receipt and recover across interruption boundaries.
- Operator-facing `start`, `attach`, `status`, `list` and `finish` behavior is documented.

We have also successfully exercised 13 credential-free adversarial scenarios, including:

- detaching and finishing;
- killing workers;
- restarting supervisors;
- denying network access;
- searching for and attempting to forge gate authority;
- Docker completion, cancellation and worker recovery;
- receipt mutation;
- result delivery;
- unified Job journeys;
- planner and child ownership;
- semantic parent repair;
- repair-lineage tampering.

The checked-in evidence reports **13 passed, 0 failed and 8 explicitly unproven**, bound to a clean source revision. See [credential-free-results.json](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/examples/watchkeeper-dogfood/credential-free-results.json).

The newest work also adds a resumable 24-task dogfood runner, strict matrix-aware metrics, human-review requirements and authenticated live sandbox observations. Its focused verification is green:

- 53 Python harness tests
- 10 Rust dogfood tests
- 11 trusted-capture tests
- 1 portability test
- formatting and warning-free clippy checks

Integration status:

- 16 goal-run commits are on `origin/main`.
- Another 6 commits are on local `main`, which is six commits ahead of GitHub.
- The newest dogfood and observation work spans 13 files and is not yet committed.
- Existing unrelated workspace changes remain isolated and have not been included.

What we have not successfully proven yet:

- the complete 24-task multi-repository/provider dogfood matrix;
- live provider worker-kill, supervisor-restart and network-loss trials;
- recovery after a genuine machine reboot with an installed user service;
- a live hostile cross-provider gate attack;
- naturally triggered semantic revise/repair;
- live Campaign interruption recovery;
- Linux `bubblewrap` isolation;
- release signing/notarization and remote CI after pushing.

So the honest conclusion is: **the durable, bounded, independently verified execution system has been implemented and strongly tested locally. The full product promise is not yet accepted because the external live trials and final integration have not happened.** The goal therefore correctly remains active.

The causes are now pinned down:

- `run.sh` trusted `dispatched.ids[0]` and interpolated it into a filesystem path without validating the 32-hex Job format.

- The same collector derived semantic evidence from `attempt.proof.marker_path` without proving that path belongs to the observed Job under `DEADRECKON_HOME`.

I’ll fix these at the input/provenance boundaries and add regression tests that reproduce each exploit.

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-07-31 11:59:06Z)**_

The honest summary: we have successfully built most of the core product promise. What remains is primarily integration and real-world proof—not another major architectural subsystem.

### Successfully implemented

- A durable job executor that detaches work, assigns one job identity, leases execution, renews heartbeats, reclaims abandoned work, and prevents stale workers from committing.
- Explicit terminal outcomes including completed, blocked, cancelled, failed and budget/time exhaustion.
- Runs, plans, chains and campaigns supervised through the same job lifecycle, including crash recovery and ownership boundaries.
- Two-key completion:
  1. deterministic definition-of-done checks;
  2. an independent, read-only semantic LLM judge.
- Semantic results of `achieved`, `revise` and `uncertain`, including bounded repair attempts. A semantic judge cannot override failing checks.
- Strict completion that fails closed to `NEEDS REVIEW` when verification or receipt sealing is unavailable.
- HMAC-SHA-256-protected gate evidence with signing material outside the agent workspace.
- Tamper-resistant receipts bound to the contract, policy, source/result revisions, semantic judgment, sandbox observation and repair lineage.
- Sandbox and control-plane protections covering macOS Seatbelt, Docker, provider routes and the Linux/bwrap implementation path.
- Process-tree and container cleanup for cancellation, worker death and supervisor recovery.
- An append-only authenticated operator history and reconstructed job/run views.
- A resumable 20–30-task dogfood runner with dry-run defaults, bounded spend, exact matrix hashing, atomic task claiming and crash-safe continuation.
- Metrics that fail closed on missing, malformed, symlinked or externally redirected evidence.

### Evidence obtained

The checked-in credential-free adversarial run currently reports:

- 13 scenarios passed
- 0 failed
- 8 honestly marked unproven
- 39 supporting commands completed successfully

Those passing scenarios include detachment, simulated worker and supervisor interruption, network denial, gate-forgery attempts, Docker control-boundary attacks, receipt mutation, unified job journeys, planner ownership, semantic repair and repair-lineage tampering.

The complete workspace test suite passed on the exact current source today. The focused Python suite also passes all 58 tests, alongside formatting, linting and focused Rust Watchkeeper tests.

### What is not yet complete

- The newest dogfood and evidence-hardening slice is reviewed and test-green, but is still uncommitted.
- Local `main` already contains six committed goal changes that have not been pushed to `origin/main`.
- We must commit the current allowlisted files, run `make verify` from that committed source, and regenerate clean-source adversarial evidence.
- The full dogfood matrix is not complete: only 2 of 24 tasks have been attempted, none yet count as human-reviewed verified trials.
- Eight live claims still need operator/environment proof: real provider worker death, supervisor restart, network loss, machine reboot, cross-provider gate attack, natural semantic repair, campaign recovery and Linux/bwrap isolation.
- Remote CI, release signing and publication are outside the completed work.

So the product is now largely feature-complete for the stated promise, but the goal run is not finished. We are at the “commit the final harness, produce clean evidence, then conduct live acceptance trials” stage. The detailed state is recorded in [MAP-OF-DEADRECKON.md](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/MAP-OF-DEADRECKON.md) and the [operator acceptance checklist](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/WATCHKEEPER-OPERATOR-ACCEPTANCE.md).

The cause is now pinned down: [ui.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon/src/ui.rs:525) prefers the controlling terminal’s real width over `COLUMNS`, while the characterization helper only sets `COLUMNS=120`. I launched `make verify` inside an 80-column PTY, so two captured child processes wrapped paths at 80 columns. The same tests pass without a controlling TTY and also pass in a 120-column PTY. This is a launch-context artifact, not a change in the committed feature behavior, so I’m leaving the source untouched and rerunning the canonical gate non-interactively, as CI does.

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-07-31 12:38:01Z)**_

Short version: we have built the core of the promise. We have not yet proven the entire promise under real operating conditions.

Successfully implemented:

- One durable outer Job lifecycle for direct runs, orchestration, new chains, plan forks, campaigns, and follow-ups.
- `start`, `attach`, `status`, `list`, `kill`, `finish`, and `report` operate through the same durable Job identity.
- Jobs are recorded before work begins, detach from the terminal, use renewable fenced leases, and retain append-only lifecycle history.
- Explicit terminal outcomes distinguish success, blocked, cancelled, failed, budget exhausted, timed out, and needs review.
- Wall-time, spend, attempt, and retry limits remain authoritative across recovery.
- Deterministic checks run inside a real sandbox and cannot be overridden by an LLM.
- A separate read-only semantic judgment must return evidence-backed `achieved`; `revise`, `uncertain`, malformed, or unavailable results are handled explicitly.
- HMAC-SHA-256 receipts bind the approved goal, contract, policy, source/result revisions and trees, sandbox observation, deterministic result, semantic judgment, and promotion.
- Gate secrets and proof paths are kept outside the worker-visible workspace, with hostile path, symlink, forged receipt, environment leakage, and tampering protections.
- Graph and Campaign results are verified at the merged parent, including bounded semantic repair without rerunning successful children.
- `finish` revalidates the receipt and resulting files before promotion.
- Managed launchd/systemd supervisor commands and definitions now exist.
- A 24-task dogfood matrix, metrics collector, protected live-trial recorder, and adversarial test suite now exist.

Successfully proven from clean committed source:

- Full workspace tests and the complete `make verify` pipeline pass.
- The clean adversarial record reports **13 passed, 0 failed, 8 explicitly unproven**.
- Real macOS Seatbelt isolation passed.
- Real Docker boundary tests passed.
- Strict Docker Job tests proved:
  - deterministic completion followed by semantic `NEEDS_REVIEW`;
  - cancellation with no retry or receipt;
  - worker `SIGKILL` cleanup followed by exactly one bounded retry.
- That evidence is bound to source commit `e87c70f` and evidence commit `e7b9bb2`.

What remains unproven:

- Live provider worker death.
- Live supervisor restart.
- Provider network loss.
- Actual machine reboot/service recovery.
- Hostile cross-provider gate attack.
- Natural semantic parent repair with real providers.
- Live Campaign interruption recovery.
- Linux/bubblewrap isolation.
- The full 24-task provider matrix: currently 2 tasks were attempted, none verified, and 22 were not run.
- Therefore we do not yet know real false-accept/reject rates, operator intervention rate, judging cost, or comprehension time.

The audits also found two smaller unfinished issues:

- A cancellation race can make `kill` report failure even though the Job correctly reaches `Cancelled` and cleanup succeeds.
- One operator-checklist command derives the capture revision from the wrong repository when the target Job belongs to a fixture clone.

The latest work is on local `main`, currently **9 commits ahead of `origin/main` and not pushed**. The goal correctly remains active. In plain language: the machinery is largely built and credibly tested; the remaining work is real-world acceptance, several destructive or provider-backed fault drills, and closing the two newly identified edge cases.

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-07-31 12:38:22Z)**_

I’m continuing with the two concrete gaps the audits just exposed: make cancellation cleanup idempotent under supervisor/operator races, then correct the live-trial revision binding so operator evidence targets the Job’s approved source rather than whichever checkout runs the recorder. After that I’ll rerun the focused and full verification suites.

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-07-31 13:07:14Z)**_

The short version: we have successfully built most of the core DeadReckon/Watchkeeper system. What remains is completing a few boundaries and proving the whole promise under real interruption conditions.

Successfully implemented and verified:

- One durable Job model. `start`, direct runs, orchestration, campaigns, supported chains, forks and follow-ups now converge on durable Jobs with stable IDs.
- Detached supervision. Jobs have fenced leases, retries, cancellation, recovery and explicit terminal outcomes.
- Two-key completion. Deterministic checks must pass, then an independent semantic judge must return an evidence-backed `achieved`. The judge cannot override failed checks.
- Tamper-resistant completion receipts. HMAC-SHA-256 receipts bind the goal, contract, policy, source/result identity, deterministic proof, semantic judgment and actual sandbox.
- Isolated gate execution. Workers cannot access signing keys or mint completion proofs. Gate inputs, lifecycle paths and receipt paths are protected.
- Crash-safe execution. Evaluator and worker identities are persisted so cancellation and recovery can clean up the correct process or Docker container without accidentally touching another Job.
- Parent verification for Graphs and Campaigns. The merged parent result—not merely successful leaves—must pass the deterministic gate and semantic judge.
- Durable semantic repair. A `revise` decision can launch bounded repair work without rerunning already-successful leaves; crash recovery avoids duplicate repair launches.
- Safe result delivery. `finish` validates the receipt and result identity before exporting work, with rollback protection if delivery validation fails.
- Operator lifecycle commands. `attach`, `status`, `list`, `kill`, `finish`, `report`, and supervisor service management operate on the durable Job.
- Dogfood and adversarial infrastructure. We have a 24-task operator matrix, metrics collector, protected evidence recorder and hostile tampering tests.
- Clean automated evidence. The last clean source recorded 13 passing proof groups, 0 failures and 39 successful authoritative commands. Eight real-world claims remained explicitly unproven rather than being falsely presented as passed.
- Full verification passed at the last clean committed source, including the workspace suite and `make verify`.

We have also completed and focused-tested three newer fixes that are not committed yet:

- Cancellation cleanup is idempotent under concurrent record removal and refuses foreign or swapped Docker execution records.
- Live evidence now derives the source revision from immutable Job authority and verifies that the selected trial matches the Job’s actual shape.
- Central Job creation now rejects invalid zero, negative or non-finite spend, wall-time and retry limits before persisting anything.

What is currently underway, so I am not counting it as successfully finished:

- Public `--deadline` support across every durable creation route.
- Authenticated “expected negative outcome” evidence, such as proving that a network-loss trial correctly ended `blocked` or `budget_exhausted` without pretending the Job was verified.
- Supervisor-service preflight on the main `start` path.
- Authoritative network-loss and Campaign-recovery trials.
- The real 24-task provider matrix, Linux/bubblewrap run and machine-reboot drill.
- A fresh full-suite run and clean evidence regeneration after the current edits.

Repository state: the goal spans 24 commits. The newest 9 commits are on local `main` but have not been pushed to `origin/main`; the deadline and negative-outcome work is still uncommitted.

So the honest assessment is: the durable execution and verification engine now exists and has substantial automated proof. We have not yet earned the complete claim that it survives every promised real-world interruption unattended. That last portion is now mostly integration, operator-boundary work and live fault validation—not invention of the core architecture.

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-07-31 14:05:47Z)**_

The short version: we have built most of DeadReckon’s durable execution spine. The goal is still active because the final live recovery proof and integration pass are not complete.

### Successfully implemented and committed locally

- One durable Job model for ordinary runs, orchestrations, stored-plan forks, supported chains, campaigns and follow-up runs.
- Immutable Job authority plus an append-only event history as lifecycle truth.
- Fenced leases, abandoned-lease recovery and protection against two supervisors owning the same Job.
- Detached execution that survives the launching terminal closing.
- Typed terminal outcomes: verified, blocked, cancelled, failed, budget exhausted, retry exhausted and needs review.
- Enforced attempt, time and spend limits.
- Isolation through worktrees and supported sandbox backends.
- Two-key completion:
  1. deterministic checks must pass;
  2. a fresh, read-only semantic judge must say the goal was achieved.
- HMAC-authenticated completion receipts bound to the Job, contract, policy, source revision, result and semantic judgment.
- Fail-closed promotion: `finish` revalidates the receipt and result before exporting work.
- Normal operator controls through `start`, `attach`, `status`, `list`, cancellation and `finish`.
- Durable parent verification and bounded semantic repair for Graph and Campaign Jobs.
- Supervisor service install/start/status/stop commands for launchd and systemd.
- Adversarial tests for receipt tampering, protected paths, lease races, process recovery, cancellation and promotion refusal.

The architecture summary is captured in [MAP-OF-DEADRECKON.md](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/MAP-OF-DEADRECKON.md:86) and the concrete execution routes in [AS-BUILT-ARCHITECTURE.md](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/AS-BUILT-ARCHITECTURE.md:4129).

### Successfully implemented in the current working tree

These have focused passing tests but are not committed yet:

- Safer cancellation cleanup that refuses foreign or swapped Docker execution records.
- Exact source-revision and Job-shape binding for live evidence.
- Central validation rejecting zero or invalid time, spend and attempt policies.
- Public `--deadline` support across run, start, orchestration, campaign, chain, plan and follow-up routes.
- Authenticated proof for expected negative outcomes such as cancellation or budget exhaustion—not only successful completion.
- Much stronger supervisor identity checks: live PID/start identity, boot identity, service configuration verification, symlink refusal and fresh-instance checks.

### What is still underway

Three workstreams are active in the shared local working tree:

- Completing the supervisor-service test fixture and adapting all real `start --yes` tests.
- Finishing and verifying the hardened service-preflight implementation.
- Replacing generic network-failure evidence with signed, attempt-bound proof of the exact provider endpoint becoming unreachable and recovering.

After those, the remaining engineering work is:

- Strengthen the Campaign interruption/recovery oracle.
- Run the complete workspace suite, clippy, formatting and `make verify`.
- Commit the current hardening changes.
- Regenerate evidence against that clean committed source.
- Run the operator-approved live trials: provider runs, network interruption, Linux/bubblewrap, machine reboot and hostile gate-tampering exercises.

### Honest evidence status

The last clean credential-free run recorded:

- 13 passed claim groups
- 0 failed
- 8 deliberately marked unproven

The live operator matrix contains 24 tasks, but only 2 have been attempted and neither reached verified completion. That is recorded in [trial-results.json](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/examples/watchkeeper-dogfood/trial-results.json:1).

Repository integration status:

- The goal spans 24 commits.
- Local `main` is currently 9 commits ahead of `origin/main`.
- Current hardening work is uncommitted and shared directly by the active agents.
- Nothing has been pushed during this run.

So the central product now exists. What remains is proving the strongest wording—especially machine-restart, network-loss and Campaign recovery—under real hostile conditions, then producing one clean, fully verified integration commit.

Probably not the entire goal today. I think we can land the current implementation slice today, but I would not yet promise the full definition of done.

What is already strong:

- Ten goal-related commits are on local `main`.
- Durable job supervision, leasing, recovery, isolation, deterministic checks, semantic judging, and signed receipts are substantially implemented.
- The current uncommitted slice adds stronger Plan fencing, isolated ordered workspaces, protected evidence paths, trustworthy marker rendering, and real detach/supervisor-race tests.
- Chain hooks now have frozen identities and durable evidence, and they fail closed rather than silently disappearing.

What still prevents a truthful completion claim:

- Wire actual chain-hook execution into the durable graph worker.
- Implement verified Job-ID undo.
- Finish judge/gate/sealing crash tests and signing-key lifecycle checks.
- Run the complete integrated verification suite.
- Complete clean end-to-end adversarial dogfooding and the operator acceptance checklist.

So my forecast is:

- **Current large slice integrated and committed today:** likely.
- **Every word of the final product promise independently proven today:** possible, but unlikely.
- **Realistic strict completion:** another focused day or two, depending on what integrated tests uncover.

what will deadreckon be able to do that it was not able to do before

---

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-07-31 16:53:57Z)**_

The practical difference is that DeadReckon will become a durable operator, not just a wrapper around a coding CLI.

You will be able to give it a goal plus an approved definition of done, receive a Job ID immediately, close the terminal, and expect the work to continue in an isolated workspace. If the worker or supervisor dies, it can recover from recorded history instead of forgetting where it was.

More specifically, it will be able to:

- Run ordinary tasks, plans, and chains through the same durable Job lifecycle.
- Prevent two supervisors from executing the same work simultaneously.
- Stop for named reasons such as blocked, cancelled, out of budget, out of time, failed, or needs review.
- Require both deterministic checks and an independent read-only semantic judgment before calling work complete.
- Keep the agent away from the policy, signing key, gate evidence, and receipt it would otherwise be able to tamper with.
- Leave a signed receipt binding the approved goal, checks, source revision, result revision, policy, judge decision, and delivery.
- Preserve ordered chain behavior inside an isolated candidate repository, without incrementally modifying your checkout.
- Freeze chain hooks before launch, run each approved hook once, and block rather than replay it when a crash leaves its external effect uncertain.
- Undo the exact revision delivered by a verified Job, rather than trusting mutable or ambiguous run state.
- Let you understand the outcome through `status`, `attach`, and `finish` without reconstructing it from logs.

Before this work, pieces of that existed, but they were split across runs, plans, campaigns, chains, mutable projections, and process-local conductors. The important new capability is the combined guarantee: **detached execution + crash recovery + isolation + bounded stopping + independent verification + a trustworthy receipt**.

Most of that foundation is now implemented. I am currently wiring the last chain-hook execution/recovery seam, while the parallel lane implements verified Job-ID undo; neither is being counted as finished until the integrated tests prove it.

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-07-31 17:10:09Z)**_

The big change is this:

> DeadReckon is becoming a durable local execution system, rather than a CLI wrapper that must remain alive while another coding agent works.

| Before | After these enhancements |
|---|---|
| Execution was closely tied to the active terminal/process. | `start` creates a Job, returns its ID and detaches. |
| An interruption could strand the work. | A supervisor can reclaim abandoned work and continue it without running it twice. |
| Runs, Plans and Chains had different lifecycle machinery. | They use the same Job, scheduler, history and receipt model. |
| Passing compiled checks could be treated as completion. | Completion requires both deterministic checks and an independent semantic judge. |
| An unavailable judge could leave an ambiguous result. | It becomes `NEEDS REVIEW`, never silently accepted. |
| Work could reach the repository through several paths. | Work stays in an isolated candidate workspace until verification permits delivery. |
| Evidence documented what happened but had weaker trust boundaries. | A signed receipt binds the goal, definition of done, policy, source revision, result revision, checks, judgment and delivery. |
| Hooks could create uncertain side effects after a crash. | Hook definitions are frozen, invocations recorded, and uncertain outcomes block recovery safely. |
| Undo was tied to older run/chain concepts. | `deadreckon undo <job-id>` reverts exactly the revision proven by that Job’s receipt. |
| Failure was often a generic execution failure. | Jobs stop for explicit reasons such as blocked, cancelled, failed, budget exhausted or needs review. |

A practical future interaction looks like:

```text
deadreckon start goal.md
Created job job_1234

# The terminal may close.

deadreckon status job_1234
deadreckon attach job_1234
deadreckon finish job_1234
```

DeadReckon will retain the history needed to answer:

- What did the agent try?
- What changed?
- Which checks passed?
- Did the result actually satisfy the stated goal?
- Why did execution stop?
- Was anything delivered to the real repository?
- Can that exact delivery be safely undone?

The most important new ability is not merely “keep an agent running.” It is:

> Keep an agent working independently while preserving enough authority, evidence and recovery state that DeadReckon can decide whether the result is safe to accept.

The honest current status is that most of the durable Job, isolation, verification, receipt and recovery foundation has landed. The current worktree also contains the new durable Chain-hook integration and Job-ID undo; it compiles, but still needs focused tests, full repository verification and a commit. Real reboot acceptance, additional judge/gate crash tests, signing-key lifecycle hardening and final adversarial dogfooding remain before we can claim the entire promise is proven end to end.

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-07-31 17:35:35Z)**_

The practical difference is this:

> You will be able to give DeadReckon an approved goal, close the terminal, and trust it to continue working until it either proves completion or stops for a precise, bounded reason.

Previously, DeadReckon could run agents, evaluate goals and collect evidence, but much of the reliability depended on the original process remaining alive. The new version adds:

- **Detached execution:** `deadreckon start` returns a Job ID while work continues independently.
- **Interruption recovery:** a supervisor can reclaim work after a terminal closes, a process crashes or a lease is abandoned—without accidentally running the agent twice.
- **Isolated workspaces:** changes are prepared away from the destination repository and only promoted after approval checks.
- **Bounded stopping:** jobs clearly end as verified, blocked, cancelled, failed, budget-exhausted or needing review.
- **Two-part verification:** deterministic checks must pass, and an independent semantic judge must agree that the result actually satisfies the goal’s meaning.
- **Tamper-resistant receipts:** the final record is signed and tied to the goal, definition of done, source revision, resulting revision, evidence and policy.
- **Safe delivery and undo:** promotion is recorded as a signed operation bound to the exact repository and Git ref, allowing DeadReckon to reverse its own delivered change safely.
- **Durable plans and chains:** multi-step work uses the same recoverable Job machinery instead of a separate, less reliable execution path.
- **Crash-safe completion:** if DeadReckon crashes between verification and recording the final state, it can recover the existing result instead of rerunning the provider.
- **Auditable explanation:** operators get a coherent account of what ran, what changed, which checks passed, what the judge concluded, how much it cost and why execution stopped.

The largest change is therefore not “more agent features.” It is moving from **a CLI session that attempts a goal** to **a local durable job system that can be entrusted with a goal**.

We have built most of that machinery. The remaining work is primarily proving and hardening the dangerous boundaries—promotion, undo, hooks, tampering and hostile crash timing—plus live restart and adversarial dogfood testing. Until those tests pass, I would describe the capability as substantially implemented but not yet fully trustworthy for unattended production use.

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-07-31 17:58:47Z)**_

When this work is finished, DeadReckon will move from “run an agent with a goal” to “own that goal until it reaches a trustworthy stopping point.”

It will be able to:

- Start work in an isolated workspace and detach from your terminal.
- Keep running after the terminal closes and resume after process or machine interruption.
- Recover abandoned work without accidentally accepting stale results.
- Enforce explicit limits for time, spending and retry attempts.
- Stop with a precise reason: verified, blocked, cancelled, timed out, budget exhausted, retry exhausted, failed or needs human review.
- Require two independent forms of completion:
  1. The compiled deterministic checks pass.
  2. A read-only LLM judge confirms that the result actually satisfies the intended goal.
- Refuse completion when either form of evidence is missing, inconsistent or tampered with.
- Treat ordinary runs, plans and chains as the same kind of durable job.
- Safely deliver a verified result back to the target repository and support undoing that delivery.
- Leave a signed, tamper-resistant receipt tying together the goal, definition of done, attempt, source revision, resulting revision, checks and semantic judgment.
- Give you one understandable place to inspect what happened, what it cost, why it stopped and what to do next.

Previously, DeadReckon could run goal-driven agent loops and collect useful evidence, but too much depended on the original process staying alive, lifecycle truth was spread across several systems, and completion evidence was not consistently protected against crashes, stale state or tampering.

Most of the underlying implementation now exists. The remaining work is primarily integrated verification, hostile crash/tamper testing and real operator dogfooding. Until that evidence is complete, the honest claim is “substantially implemented,” not yet “proven dependable.”

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-07-31 17:59:13Z)**_

The immediate checkpoint is to integrate the shared job-operation lock with the receipt/recovery hardening, compile the combined worktree, and repair any cross-feature regressions before adding the remaining crash and tamper evidence.

The goal that kicked this work off was:

> Give DeadReckon an approved goal and definition of done. It should work in an isolated workspace, keep going across interruptions, stop only for explicit bounded reasons, independently verify both the checks and the meaning of the result, and leave behind a clear, tamper-resistant receipt explaining what happened.

That translated into five main outcomes:

- Durable jobs that survive process or machine interruption.
- Deterministic checks plus an independent semantic LLM judge.
- Hardened gates and receipts that the working agent cannot forge.
- One consistent job model for runs, plans, chains and campaigns.
- Adversarial dogfooding to prove recovery, bounded stopping and tamper resistance.

The overarching promise was: you should be able to give another coding CLI a goal and confidently leave DeadReckon supervising it until it either proves completion or stops for a precise, honest reason.
